claim: Citations to a patent rise with the familiarity of its components (+11.3% per SD; +147% from lowest to highest) in Fleming's 17,264-patent sample. The same direction shows in paper-wide data using conventionality-like measures (Uzzi: conventional core; Mukherjee: recent-and-varied sources).
agent_test: Compare candidate blends built from familiar parts versus unfamiliar parts at equal tokens; score by a held-out usefulness check, not by novelty.
audit_note: Fleming 2001 (n=17,264; +147% lowest to highest; +11.3% per SD) and Uzzi (conventional core) verified; Mukherjee's recent-and-varied-age sources is not really a conventionality/familiarity measure, so 'same direction' is a loose analogy.

claim: Reworking a combination that has been used before raises mean usefulness and lowers spread. The spread cut is tiny at the average patent (2.2%) and large only at extreme reuse (64%). One paper (Fleming 2001); no independent replication of this half found. Full text re-opened (d01): numbers confirmed.
agent_test: Arm A: refine one blend for k rounds. Arm B: draw k fresh blends. Equal tokens; compare mean and SD of verified usefulness.

claim: Cumulative reuse of the same combination lowers the usefulness of the next invention that uses it (37.9% of baseline at max use). Fleming cannot separate this from normal life-cycle decline.
agent_test: Track how often a pair has been tried in this run; test whether a penalty on repeated pairs raises best-of-N at equal tokens.

claim: New combinations have wider outcome spread (fatter top and bottom tails). Seen in patents (Verhoeven: 3.3% base rate at +2SD, up to 6.48x for all-three novelty) and in papers (Wang: dispersion +14.90%, top-10% odds +16.80%, bottom-10% odds +16.76%).
agent_test: Check that novel-pair blends give higher variance of a verified score than familiar-pair blends; if so, add a cheap screen before spending tokens on execution.
audit_note: Wang/Veugelers/Stephan (dispersion +14.90%, top-10% +16.80%, bottom-10% +16.76%) and Verhoeven/Bakker/Veugelers (3.3% base, 6.48x for all three) verified; share co-author Veugelers but are separate datasets/studies.

claim: The lower-mean half of Fleming's claim is split by unit and by controls. Papers: novel work has HIGHER mean citations (Wang 2017: +12.04%; +2.78% moderate; only with long windows), and Foster finds higher mean for rarer strategies. Patents: Fleming (1990 US cohort) and Verhoeven 2016 (PATSTAT families, N = 2.3 to 3.6 million) both find a lower mean for new combinations AFTER controls (new recombination -9.1%, new technological origins -11.9%), yet raw means are higher for novel patents (any flag 6.62 vs 6.03; all three 12.96 vs 6.17). New scientific origins raise the mean (+4.8%).
agent_test: Do not assume novelty lowers mean quality for the agent. Measure it: mean verified score of far-pair vs near-pair blends.

claim: Impact peaks when a work is mostly conventional plus a small tail of unusual combinations: hit rate per 100 is 9.11 (conventional core + novel tail) vs 5.82 conventional only, 5.33 novel only, 2.05 neither (17.9M papers). Mukherjee (recent knowledge with wide age spread, 2.2x hits) points the same way.
agent_test: Mixed blend policy: mostly near, familiar pairs with one or two far components. Compare to all-near and all-far at equal tokens.
audit_note: Uzzi et al. 2013 hit rates 9.11/5.82/5.33/2.05 of 17.9M papers and Mukherjee hotspot 2.2x (28.4M papers) verified.

claim: Journal-pair novelty measures are coarse. Bornmann finds the Uzzi-style score tracks expert novelty tags (+7.47% per SD, but pseudo R2 0.33%) and the Wang-style score does not; Fontana finds first-appearance novelty mostly reflects citation-network structure.
agent_test: Do not use journal-pair distance as the agent's distance metric without checking it against a task outcome.
audit_note: Bornmann et al. (+7.47% per SD for U, pseudo R2 0.33%, n=23,206; W mostly not) verified; Fontana et al. abstract says first-appearance novelty captures structural properties of the citation network and struggles to separate novel from non-novel (validation results not in abstract).

claim: Atypical references go with LOWER disruption across 19M papers (coefficient -0.0009 in 2,461 version pairs). Extending into a new topic and displacing a dominant idea are different outcomes. Preprints, one group.
agent_test: Separate two goals in tests: extend into a new topic (far blend) versus replace the current best idea (targeted rework). Score each with its own metric.

claim: Rarer research moves earn more citations on average but the extra reward does not cover the extra risk of going unpublished; scientists mostly repeat (85.8% repeat, 14.2% new). Single large study. Manuscript text re-opened (d04): 85.8/14.2 and 2.26 extra citations confirmed; surprisal explains 29.2% of mean-citation variation and 28.6% of the spread.
agent_test: Allocate a small fixed share of budget (about 10-15%) to far moves; test the share at equal tokens.

claim: Patents that cite scientific papers get 49% more 10-year citations and 117% higher odds of being top-5% hits (171% for top 1%) in Ke et al.; among them, citing more recent science adds further impact, but that gain is offset when the cited papers' ages have low variance (Mukherjee et al.: recent and age-varied sources are about 2.2 times as likely to be top 5%).
agent_test: When retrieving inspiration, force age or source diversity in the retrieved set; compare to top-k nearest at equal tokens.
audit_note: Ke et al. (+49% 10-year citations, +117% top-5% odds, +171% top-1%) and Mukherjee (2.2x) verified, but the +49%/+117% belong to patents citing science at all; recency adds to this and low age variance offsets the recency gain, so 'only when recent and varied' is wrong.
claim_before_audit: Patents that cite science do better (+49% 10-year citations, +117% odds of top-5%), but only when the sources are recent and varied in age; low age variance offsets the benefit. Holds across thresholds (+171% for top 1%). Re-opened and confirmed.

claim: Combinations in real invention keep growing steadily: about 60% of new US patents make a never-seen combination, 40% reuse one; reuse is highly uneven.
agent_test: Background only; no direct agent test.
audit_note: Youn et al. verified (C=0.6P, 60% new combinations and 40% reuse, heavy-tailed use); Tria et al. is a model on non-patent data, so only Youn supports the patent numbers.

claim: Collaboration adds unusual combinations without losing the conventional core (tail novelty 36.2%, 39.9%, 49.7% for solo, two, three or more authors; printed Science text, d03). Singh-Fleming's 'cut the poor tail, lift the good tail' is still abstract-only (full text not reachable, d08). In 50 million works, bigger teams give more hits but less disruption, and cross-journal fusion peaks at 8 to 10 members (Wu 2019, d07). For LLM agents, outputs from different models and repeated samples are highly similar (d09), so several agents are not independent searchers. Sources differ on mechanism.
agent_test: Several independent agents proposing blends, pooled and screened, vs one agent with the same tokens.

claim: LLMs given a random far source domain produce more original product ideas than humans, and originality rises with source-target distance (LLM slope b=.18, human b=.1). For the two best models the cross-domain benefit is not significant over all pairs (b=0.02, p=.64) and appears only for the most distant 50% (b=0.12) or 10% (b=0.24). Re-opened and confirmed. Pooled over seven LLMs the supplied far source first underperformed a plain user-need prompt and became non-significant once the nearest 20% of pairs were removed; Llama-3.3-70b did not reliably beat humans; no per-open-weight threshold and one task only (d15).
agent_test: Sweep analogue distance in bins at equal tokens; look for the threshold where the gain appears.

claim: Fleming's cost of novelty shows in humans but not LLMs: the top 10% most original human cross-domain ideas had lower utility (b=0.81), investment-worthiness (0.60) and feasibility (0.26) than equally original LLM ideas. Humans copy surface features, LLMs copy structure. Re-opened and confirmed (tail was selected).
agent_test: Check whether agent far blends keep feasibility; a separate feasibility check is still needed because this is one study with a selected tail.

claim: Structured analogical reasoning (build a relational analogy, then solve in the analog) raises domain distance over 3x and solution diversity (Vendi +90-173%) over just asking for cross-domain ideas, which barely helps. Judging is by an LLM with moderate human agreement; humans found 67% reasonable.
agent_test: Compare a plain 'use another domain' prompt with an explicit abstract-structure-then-map step at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs fixate on the same parts when asked to blend: GPT-4o used smoked paprika in 56% of recipes vs 0.375% in the corpus; 47% of its outputs have similarity over 0.85 to a corpus recipe. A recombination scaffold (trees, edits, value threshold) raised novelty (3.53 vs 3.146) at some value cost (85% vs 98% valued in Exp 2). Budget caveat (d14): the pipeline kept the top 5 of up to 5,600 trees per pair (about $42 per step) against 5 recipes from one prompted session, so the comparison is not at equal tokens and has no best-of-N arm.
agent_test: Measure part repetition across N blends from the agent; test explicit part-ranking and a value threshold against free generation.

claim: Higher temperature makes new combinations cheaply but not combinations outside what artists already use; explicit ranking by unavailability does. Peeperkorn (second-hand only) reports a weak, limited link between temperature and novelty.
agent_test: Compare temperature-raising with explicit rare-pair ranking at equal tokens.

claim: LLM-generated research ideas are rated more novel by blinded experts (5.64 vs 4.84, 79 reviewers) with no feasibility loss, but only about 5% of 4,000 seeds are non-duplicate. After execution the AI ideas lose 1.05 to 1.88 points while human ideas do not move (confirmed in the paper text).
agent_test: Always add a verification or execution-style check before ranking by novelty; dedupe across samples.

claim: LLM-rated novelty does not predict real later impact: in HINDSIGHT, LLM-judge scores are equal for grounded and vanilla ideas (7.44 vs 7.40) while matching to future papers shows a 2.5x gap (0.297 vs 0.119), and the HINDSIGHT score correlates -0.29 with LLM-judged novelty. Si et al. 2025 point the same way: AI ideas rated more novel before execution lost 1.05 novelty points and 1.88 effectiveness points after experts ran them, while human ideas lost almost none.
agent_test: Do not use LLM-judged novelty as the selection criterion. Use an external or retrieval-grounded check.
audit_note: HINDSIGHT numbers (7.44 vs 7.40, 0.297 vs 0.119, 2.5x, r=-0.29) verified, but Si 2025 does not show novelty rating surviving: AI ideas' novelty scores fell 1.05 points after execution (human -0.01), the human-AI difference at execution is non-significant on novelty simply because the AI advantage vanished.
claim_before_audit: LLM-rated novelty does not predict real later impact. HINDSIGHT finds LLM-judge scores equal for grounded and vanilla ideas (7.44 vs 7.40) while future-paper matching shows 2.5x (0.297 vs 0.119); correlation with LLM-judged novelty is -0.29. Si 2025 shows the same pattern from the other side (novelty rating survives, effectiveness falls on execution).

claim: AI research agents explore less than humans: distance from seed papers 0.322 vs 0.410, breadth 0.554 vs 0.599 (confirmed); their novelty is more method recombination than new problems. LLM hypotheses are further from the nearest paper but lower in direction (ONS 15-23% lower); distant context raises distance but not direction.
agent_test: Force distant context (farthest-papers) and measure both distance and direction; check whether blends differ in kind, not only in distance.
audit_note: Tang & Yang (distance 0.322 vs 0.410, breadth 0.554 vs 0.599, method recombination more common than new problems) and Liu et al. (ONS 15-23% lower, further from nearest paper, farthest-context effect) verified from the PDFs; Bao et al. not needed.

claim: Iterating recombination appears to have a sweet spot in one study: in Chen and Zhang, diversity and novelty peak near the second iteration while later rounds lock onto the previous version (70.6% new entities at turn 1, 78.3% inherited at turn 3). SciMON's novelty loop still raised novelty on iteration 2 (55.6% of ideas on iteration 1, 57.8% of continuing ideas on iteration 2), and Nova's planned retrieval gives 3.4 times more unique novel ideas than no framework over 3 rounds, with the no-planning ablation flat between rounds 2 and 3 (42.4 to 44.1). All judge novelty with LLMs or embeddings, not outcomes.
agent_test: Cap refinement rounds at about 2 before regenerating; test 1, 2 and 4 rounds at equal tokens.
audit_note: Chen & Zhang (70.6% new at turn 1, 78.3% inherited at turn 3, diversity/novelty peak early near iteration 2) and SciMON (55.6%, 57.8%) numbers verified, but SciMON shows gains still rising at iteration 2, not a sweet spot, and Nova's 3.4x is the framework versus no framework (only 3 rounds run), not growth over rounds; only the no-planning ablation (42.4 to 44.1) is flat.
claim_before_audit: Iterating recombination has a sweet spot. Diversity and novelty peak near the second iteration and later rounds lock onto the previous version (70.6% new at turn 1, 78.3% inherited at turn 3). Same direction as Fleming's refinement claim and SciMON's novelty loop (55.6% gain on iteration 1, 57.8% on iteration 2). Nova (d12) adds a third source: unique novel ideas rise over 3 rounds of retrieve-and-revise (3.4x) and stop after round 3; without planned retrieval the count is flat between rounds 2 and 3 (42.4 to 44.1). All three judge novelty with LLMs or embeddings, not an outcome check.

claim: Pure random enumeration of theme-domain-method triples gives high diversity but low relevance (distinct-1 0.41 vs 0.21; BLEU 0.05 vs 0.11); frequency-ranked gives the reverse. Same trade as Fleming's novelty vs usefulness.
agent_test: Test a mixed schedule of random and frequency-ranked pairs at equal tokens.

claim: Retrieval of facet-matched inspirations with a novelty check against literature works: a facet-aware checker finds 89.66% of not-novel ideas vs 10.34% for embedding-only. Near, far and very far labels agree only moderately with annotators (kappa 0.53-0.61).
agent_test: Novelty check against retrieved prior work before expensive evaluation; verify distance labels.

claim: Weitzman (1998) models growth as recombination of old ideas, with the supply of possible combinations exploding and the binding limit being the ability to process them into usable form; Tria et al. (2014) and Pichler et al. (2020) model rates of novelty and innovation (Heaps law, network dependencies) and do not address usability. Evidence in this set is about rates, not usefulness.
agent_test: Motivates budgeting for screening, not generation. No direct test.
audit_note: Only Weitzman (1998) says the bottleneck is turning ideas into usable form (PDF text not machine-readable here; abstract wording known); Tria 2014 and Pichler 2020 abstracts model rates only and say nothing of a usability bottleneck, and Arthur-Polak 2006 has no evidence line.
claim_before_audit: Models of recombinant growth (Weitzman 1998, Tria 2014, Pichler 2020, Arthur-Polak 2006) say the supply of new combinations explodes and the bottleneck is turning them into usable form. Evidence is about rates, not usefulness.

claim: Novelty and usefulness can have different search origins. Kaplan-Vakili (abstract only) say new-topic patents come from local search and valuable ones from broad recombination. Sample size disagrees across sources (2,826 vs 2,384).
agent_test: None until the full text is read.

claim: Inspirations that are near in purpose and far in mechanism, spread by a max-min rule, raised the share of good ideas over surface-near and random inspirations (46% vs 37% random vs 30% surface at 2-of-5 judges; 38% vs 22% vs 21% at 3-of-5). Surface-near retrieval was no better than random. Humans (38 workers, 749 ideas), wide intervals.
agent_test: Rank parts by goal similarity, then take mostly near-goal parts with one far-mechanism part chosen by a max-min spread. Compare with surface-near and random picks at equal tokens.

claim: Several LLM samples are not independent: on 100 open-ended queries (50 responses each, top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0) one model gave average pairwise embedding similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases, and responses from different models had average pairwise similarity of 71% to 82% (Jiang et al. 2025); in Kombine 19.9% (412 of 2,070) of invented concepts reuse two or more properties of another model concept. This suggests that more samples of one prompt or model add little spread; that diversity must come from different inputs is an inference, not a tested result.
agent_test: Compare k agents on different part sets with k agents on one part set at equal tokens; measure distinct verified solutions.
audit_note: Numbers confirmed (79%, 71-82%, 19.9%/412 of 2,070), but the 79% comes from 100 queries (Infinity-Chat100) not all 26K prompts, 71-82% is embedding similarity not agreement, and the conclusion that spread must come from different inputs is not tested by either source.
claim_before_audit: Several LLM samples are not independent: one model repeats itself (79% of prompts have average pairwise similarity above 0.8 at temperature 1), and different models agree 71% to 82% on average; 19.9% of invented concepts in Kombine reuse two or more properties of another model's concept. Spread has to come from different inputs, not from more samples of one prompt.

claim: LLM research ideas already lean on recombination: bridge or fragmentation framing in 47.1% to 64.2% of ideas across nine LLMs versus 12.1% for human papers, and explicit synthesis as the main method 22.5% to 38.7% versus 5.1%. Thinking mode raises both (Qwen3-8B bridge 49.7% to 71.1%). A blend step adds to an existing habit.
agent_test: Give the blend step a fixed share of the budget and keep a branch that reframes the problem instead of blending.

claim: A search that mostly takes the best-scoring problem-method pair but accepts a random pair with small probability found more high-disruption pairs than pure greedy search (hit rate 26.3 vs 19.3 on DBLP, 28.1 vs 21.5 PubMed, 24.6 vs 18.2 PatSnap) and than prompting GPT-4o or Claude (14.3 to 19.0). Probability unstated, index from the authors' own predictor, compute not matched.
agent_test: Sweep the share of random far moves (0, 5, 15, 30%) inside a greedy blend search at equal tokens with a verified score.

claim: Fleming (2001) full text confirms its core numbers (n = 17,264; +11.3% per SD component familiarity; +10.3% per SD combination familiarity; 37.9% of baseline at max cumulative use). Uzzi et al. print the team shares inconsistently: 36.1, 39.8 and 49.7 percent in the body text and 36.2, 39.9 and 49.7 percent in the Figure 3 caption. Foster et al. report 85.8 vs 14.2 repeat/new (arXiv preprint). Singh-Fleming 2010, Fleming-Sorenson 2001, Katila-Ahuja 2002 and Kaplan-Vakili 2015 are still unread.
agent_test: None. Source check.
audit_note: Fleming numbers confirmed in full text and Foster 85.8/14.2 found in the arXiv preprint, but the Uzzi paper itself prints both sets: body text says 36.1, 39.8, 49.7% while the Fig. 3 caption says 36.2, 39.9, 49.7%, so the earlier values are not mere transcription slips.
claim_before_audit: Fleming's own full text confirms its core numbers (n = 17,264; +11.3% per SD component familiarity; +10.3% per SD combination familiarity; 37.9% of baseline at max cumulative use). Uzzi's printed team shares are 36.2, 39.9 and 49.7 percent; the earlier 36.1 and 39.8 were slips. Foster's 85.8 vs 14.2 repeat/new split is confirmed. Singh-Fleming 2010, Fleming-Sorenson 2001, Katila-Ahuja 2002 and Kaplan-Vakili 2015 are still unread.

claim: Teams reach the conventional-core-plus-novel-tail mix more often than solo authors (d03). Large teams give more hits but less disruption, and unusual combinations across journals saturate at 8 to 10 members and then reverse (Wu 2019, 50 million works). Larger is not always better.
agent_test: Vary the number of independent agents (1, 3, 5, 9) at equal total tokens; look for saturation.
audit_note: Minor: published Nature abstract says 65 million works (manuscript wording was more than 50 million); the 8-10 member saturation is in the supplement (Fig. S4), confirmed via text quotes from search, and Uzzi team shares appear (36.1/39.8 body vs 36.2/39.9 caption) but direction holds.
